To address this limitation, we propose HelixPR (Helix-aware Periodic Representation), a biologically motivated DNA sequence representation for enhancer identification. RESULTS: HelixPR augments per-nucleotide one-hot encoding with a sinusoidal periodic encoding using a period of [Formula: see text] base pairs. It further incorporates a global nucleotide-composition token to capture sequence-level compositional information complementary to local nucleotide patterns. Together, these components form a compact, interpretable, and information-preserving representation of DNA sequences. Combined with a lightweight one-dimensional convolutional neural network, HelixPR achieved competitive performance across benchmark datasets. On Liu's benchmark, HelixPR achieved an accuracy of 0.8434 and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.6874 for enhancer identification. For enhancer strength classification, HelixPR achieved an accuracy of 0.8400 and an AUC of 0.9346, outperforming baseline methods. On Basith's benchmark, HelixPR obtained a mean balanced accuracy of 0.9778, substantially outperforming existing methods. Further analysis showed that HelixPR supports closed-form decoding and that HelixPR-highlighted regions are enriched for known transcription-factor binding motifs, supporting both the interpretability and biological relevance of the proposed representation. CONCLUSIONS: These results suggest that incorporating the periodic structure of the DNA double helix can improve enhancer modeling. By combining nucleotide identity, helical periodicity, and global compositional information, HelixPR offers a biologically grounded framework for enhancer identification and related regulatory sequence prediction tasks.

title: Sinomenine prevents monocrotaline-induced pulmonary arterial hypertension by inhibiting osteopontin-mediated PASMC phenotypic switching.
authors: Zeng, Zhenhua; Chen, Ziyi; Liu, Jianxin; Xu, Wen; Qin, Yao; Lin, Xinyi; Wu, Weihua; Zhou, Hua; Huang, Xiaoyang
abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a life-threatening disease driven by progressive pulmonary vascular remodeling, and aberrant phenotypic transition of pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cells (PASMCs) serves as the core pathological driver of disease deterioration. Sinomenine (SIN), a structurally defined isoquinoline alkaloid isolated from Sinomenium acutum (Thunb.) Rehder & E.H.Wilson, exhibits anti-inflammatory, vascular-protective, and anti-remodeling activities. Nevertheless, the exact molecular mechanism by which SIN regulates PASMC dysfunction to prevent PAH remains unclear. In vivo, SIN administration significantly attenuated MCT-induced PAH, right ventricular hypertrophy and pulmonary vascular remodeling in rats. In vitro, SIN effectively suppressed platelet-derived growth factor-BB (PDGF-BB)-triggered proliferation, migration and phenotypic switching of PASMCs. RNA-sequencing coupled with KEGG enrichment analysis further identified the ECM-receptor interaction pathway as the key signaling cascade dysregulated by MCT, with osteopontin (OPN) validated as the central functional target of SIN. OPN overexpression recapitulated the pro-remodeling effects of PDGF-BB in PASMCs, and such abnormal phenotypes were prevented by SIN. Molecular docking and cellular thermal shift assay demonstrated that SIN binds to NF-kappaB, a transcription factor of OPN, and suppresses PDGF-BB-induced NF-kappaB activation. This study uncovers a novel mechanism of SIN against PAH and highlights OPN as a critical mediator of its protective effects.

title: Formononetin disrupts MRSA biofilm via potential SarA-associated regulatory modulation.
authors: Borah, Atlanta; Jena, Jashaswi Priyadarshini; Vijay, Macha; Okram, Annie; M, Gowtham; P, Niveditha; Barbuddhe, Sukhadeo B; Hegde, Nagendra R; Rawool, Deepak B; Srivastava, Anand
abstract: Biofilm formation is a crucial aspect of Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) pathogenesis and contributes to its resistance against conventional antibiotics. This study reports the identification of a bioactive molecule, formononetin, from Glycyrrhiza glabra L., that is effective against MRSA. Formononetin significantly inhibited biofilm formation, disrupted sessile biofilm, and reduced the hemolytic activity of MRSA in a dose-dependent manner. Formononetin also increased the survival rate of MRSA-infected G. mellonella larvae by decreasing the bacterial load and increasing melanization. The combination of formononetin with antibiotics, like oxacillin, ampicillin, and streptomycin, showed a fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) </= 0.5, which indicates a synergistic effect. Molecular docking studies showed formononetin can bind to the global regulator, SarA, with an estimated binding score of -6.176 kcal/mol. Further, the aspartate residue (D20) in SarA was identified as a binding site for formononetin. Microscale thermophoresis and electrophoretic mobility shift assay of the SarAD20A mutant showed reduced affinity towards formononetin without affecting its DNA-binding activity compared to its wild-type counterpart. Further, proteomic profiling of MRSA upon treatment with formononetin showed significant modulation of SarA and SarA-related pathways, such as scdA and agrC. Our findings suggest that formononetin holds promise as a natural agent for combating MRSA biofilm.

title: Integrative Network Pharmacology and Transcriptomic Analysis Prioritizes CCR1 and C5AR1 as Candidate Thromboinflammatory Targets Shared by Panax notoginseng Saponins and Stroke-Relevant Drugs in Ischemic Stroke.
authors: Chen, Genhui; Ye, Ying; Zheng, Ronghui; Xie, Qian; Li, Fei; Yang, Wei
abstract: Thromboinflammation is a central pathological process contributing to secondary brain injury after ischemic stroke (IS). Panax notoginseng saponins (PNS) exert pleiotropic anti-inflammatory, antithrombotic, and vascular effects, but the molecular convergence between PNS-associated pharmacology and stroke-relevant conventional agents remains incompletely characterized. We integrated network pharmacology, bulk transcriptomic datasets, single-cell RNA sequencing, regulatory-network analysis, and structure-based molecular docking to prioritize candidate targets shared by PNS and an exploratory screening panel of 16 stroke-relevant pharmacological agents. Predicted drug and PNS targets were intersected with IS-associated differentially expressed genes (DEGs), followed by network analysis, independent cross-dataset expression assessment, gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA), transcription-factor (TF) prediction with co-expression analysis, myeloid-cell sub-clustering, and GNINA docking. The screening framework yielded 79 shared predicted pharmacological targets and 10 disease-associated candidates: ITK, CDK2, C5AR1, VDR, S1PR2, KIF11, CCR1, FAP, PRKCD, and MAOA. CCR1 and C5AR1 were prioritized because they combined high network connectivity with consistent disease-associated expression across the analyzed datasets and strong links to thromboinflammatory pathways. BATF2 and SPI1 expression positively correlated with both C5AR1 and CCR1 in GSE56267. Myeloid sub-clustering further showed that C5ar1 was broadly distributed across stroke-associated microglial and monocyte/macrophage states, whereas Ccr1 was more restricted to activated inflammatory and infiltrating myeloid populations. GNINA docking of all fourteen network-defined receptor-ligand systems identified five complexes with docking affinity scores between - 8.06 and - 10.94 kcal/mol (ginsenosides Rd and Re at CCR1; notoginsenoside R1, ginsenoside Rg1, and ginsenoside Rd at C5AR1). Collectively, these analyses prioritize CCR1 and C5AR1 as convergent candidate thromboinflammatory nodes shared by PNS-associated and stroke-relevant pharmacological target spaces. The findings are hypothesis-generating and do not establish pharmacological synergy, direct receptor coupling, or causal therapeutic mechanisms.

title: Drugging Pockets at the Surface of c-MYC Oncoproteins Revealed by Well-Tempered Metadynamics.
authors: Ge, Yanhong; Lu, Huixia; Marti, Jordi
journal: Journal of chemical information and modeling
abstract: The MYC oncogene encodes a master transcription factor essential for regulating cellular homeostasis, growth, and metabolism. However, its deregulation is involved in up to 70% of human cancers, where it drives uncontrolled cellular proliferation. Structurally, MYC is characterized by an N-terminal transactivation domain and a C-terminal bHLHLZ domain critical for DNA binding and dimerization with MAX. Despite its clinical significance, MYC has remained historically "undruggable" due to its intrinsically disordered structure and the absence of traditional binding pockets. In this study, we combined all-atom Molecular Dynamics and well-tempered metadynamics simulations to map the conformational landscape of a MYC motif in aqueous ionic solution. The selected energy-minimized structures exhibit stable conformations and drugging pockets, providing structural foundations for targetting c-MYC. Furthermore, both the electrostatic potential and docking results for the obtained structure and the MYC inhibitor's 10074-G5 demonstrated excellent fit, highlighting its potential as a drug target. This inhibitor, introduced in several previously unpublished drugging pockets, maintained a steady binding to MYC over unbiased trajectories lasting 1 mus. These findings provide a previously uncharacterized structural foundation for the design of innovative therapeutic interventions, such as small-molecule inhibitors or peptides aimed at disrupting oncogenic MYC activity.

title: The Scm FCS finger binds the Pcl Tudor domain to link canonical PRC1 and PRC2.1 in Drosophila.
authors: Yesil, Berfin; Steigenberger, Barbara; Bonnet, Jacques; Muller, Jurg
journal: Protein science : a publication of the Protein Society
abstract: Canonical Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 (PRC1) was previously reported to selectively associate with Polycomb Repressive Complex 2.1 (PRC2.1) in cross-linking-based affinity purification experiments from Drosophila embryos, but the molecular basis of this interaction has remained unresolved. Here, we established an affinity-purification strategy using cryo-milled Drosophila embryos that recovers intact canonical PRC1 together with the complete PRC2.1 complex without chemical cross-linking. Using AlphaFold3 to systematically model interactions between canonical PRC1 and PRC2.1 subunits, we identified a single high-confidence interface between the FCS finger of the canonical PRC1 accessory subunit Sex comb on midleg (Scm) and the atypical Tudor domain of the PRC2.1 accessory subunit Polycomblike (Pcl). Recombinant Scm FCS finger and Pcl Tudor domain formed a stable complex in vitro, as demonstrated by size-exclusion chromatography and native mass spectrometry. Structure-guided mutagenesis validated the predicted interface: point mutations in either interaction partner abolished complex formation, whereas complementary charge-reversal mutations restored binding. These findings identify the Scm-Pcl interaction as the molecular basis for the selective association between canonical PRC1 and PRC2.1 in Drosophila and reveal that communication between these complexes is mediated by a direct interaction between these accessory subunits.

title: Integrated Multi-omics Reveals Molecular Signatures of Rett Syndrome, Informing Future Biomarker Discovery.
authors: Issar, Jasmeen Kaur; Hertzog, Ashley; Pang, Ignatius; Graham, Mark E; Aryamanesh, Nader; Riley, Lisa G; Piras, Ignazio S; Hansen, Nathaniel P; Finney, Caitlin A; Shvetcov, Artur; Gloss, Brian; Bandodkar, Sushil; Dale, Russell C; Sun, Qin; Ellaway, Carolyn; Tolun, Adviye A; Ho, Gladys; Kaufmann, Walter E; Gold, Wendy A
abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder primarily caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MECP2) gene. Despite numerous clinical trials being conducted, there are limited disease-modifying options available for individuals with RTT. This paucity of effective treatments can in part be attributed to the lack of clinically useful biomarkers that can objectively assess treatment response. Moreover, diagnosis of RTT continues to be clinical, when clinical manifestations are apparent, precluding early therapeutic approaches. Thus, clinical biomarkers of disease stage could improve diagnosis and enable real-time monitoring of response to treatment, providing the earliest possible indications of therapeutic efficacy. Given MeCP2's role as a key regulator of gene transcription, we used an untargeted omics approach to evaluate transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolic profiles in blood from individuals with RTT (n = 9) and age- and sex-matched controls (n = 8). In addition to characterising differential expression at each omic layer, to understand the shared biology and coordinated molecular signals across all omic datasets, we used the unsupervised machine learning framework Multi-Omics Factor Analysis version 2 (MOFA2). The individual omic data consisted of a robust upregulation of genes involved in ribosomal structure and translation together with a downregulation in vesicle trafficking genes. An upregulation in ribosomal machinery and mitochondrial function together with a concomitant downregulation of critical epigenetic regulators, immune-signalling molecules, and cytoskeletal structural anchors was observed in the proteomics, which was supported by the phosphoproteomics. Notably, plasma metabolomics pointed towards alterations in energy substrates and lipid/cholesterol handling, suggesting systemic downstream consequences of primary intracellular disturbances. The integrated MOFA2 data supported the individual omic data revealing a central disease axis principally shaped by the proteome and transcriptome and supported by the metabolome and phosphoproteome, identifying potential biomarkers, including latent biological processes that distinguish RTT from controls (Latent Factor 1) and correlates of clinical severity (Latent Factor 2). Overall, our data reveal a distinctive 'disease state' molecular signature that distinguishes individuals with RTT from controls, where the findings in RTT blood cells are consistent with previously reported altered translational and mitochondrial function and disrupted chromatin regulation, cytoskeletal dynamics, and metabolic signalling. Our integrated multi-omics analyses revealed that PBMC's LTN1, ATRX, CHD8, SPTB, DMTN, PRF1, CD40LG, and PTPRCAP and plasma glutamate are the most promising disease-state (complementary diagnostic) candidate biomarkers while sphingomyelin, RTN3, and MMP1 appear to be the most suitable biomarkers of disease severity. Here, we demonstrate that blood from individuals with RTT reflects the molecular systemic consequences of MeCP2 dysfunction.

title: Development of a cell-penetrating peptide for intracellular delivery of a biologically active HPV E6 inhibitor in cervical cancer cells.
authors: Dassi, Luisa; Tornesello, Anna Lucia; Vincenzi, Marian; Leone, Marilisa; Ingangi, Vincenzo; Lu, Wuyuan; Cerasuolo, Andrea; Pecchillo Cimmino, Tiziana; Amiranda, Sara; Napolitano, Mariapia; Tirino, Palma; Tuccillo, Franca Maria; Buonaguro, Luigi; De Gregorio, Vincenza; Imparato, Giorgia; Buonaguro, Franco Maria; Tornesello, Maria Lina
journal: Journal of experimental & clinical cancer research : CR
abstract: BACKGROUND: The E6 oncoprotein of high-risk human papillomaviruses (HPVs) promotes cervical carcinogenesis by forming a complex with the ubiquitin ligase E6AP to mediate p53 proteasomal degradation. A 15-amino-acid peptide (pep11) was shown to disrupt the HPV16 E6/E6AP complex, to restore p53 stability and to induce apoptosis in HPV16-positive cancer cells. In this study, a short cell-penetrating peptide (CPP) was conjugated to the pep11 N-terminus to improve its solubility and intracellular delivery in HPV-positive cancer cells. METHODS: CPP-pep11 was synthesized using Boc chemistry. The interactions of CPP-pep11 with HPV16 and HPV18 E6 were modelled using AlphaFold2, while peptide structures were characterised by NMR spectroscopy. HPV16-positive SiHa and HPV18-positive C4-I cervical cancer cells were treated with CPP-pep11 (0.5-20 microM) for 24-72 h. Effects on proliferation and clonogenicity were assessed using xCELLigence and colony formation assays. Peptide uptake and localization were analysed by confocal microscopy and differential cell fractionation, while p53 expression and viability were evaluated by Western blotting and cytotoxicity assays. RESULTS: AlphaFold2 modelling suggested that CPP-pep11 can interact with both HPV16 E6 and HPV18 E6, with a more stable predicted binding to HPV16 E6. CPP-pep11 was soluble in water at 20 microM and, according to NMR analysis, predominantly adopted a disordered conformation. CPP-pep11 efficiently entered the SiHa and C4-I cell membranes, mainly localised to the cytoplasm at lower concentrations (0.5-5 microM) and to the nucleus at higher concentrations (10-20 microM). CPP-pep11 induced dose- and time-dependent inhibition of proliferation, with a significant reduction in colony formation in both cell lines. Treatment also restored p53 levels at 48 and 72 h, consistent with disruption of E6-mediated degradation. CONCLUSIONS: In conclusion, CPP-pep11 is a novel peptide-based inhibitor of HPV16 E6 and HPV18 E6 with therapeutic potential in HPV-associated malignancies by restoring p53 levels and inhibiting cancer cell proliferation.

title: Evolution-Inspired Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization for Protein Engineering.
authors: Wen, Kai; Wang, Sirui; Sun, Yixin; Li, Shiwen; Wang, Mengsong; Liu, Haoyang; Li, Quanshun; Zhu, Jingxuan
abstract: Protein engineering requires efficient navigation of vast sequence spaces under limited evaluation budgets, especially when multiple properties must be optimized simultaneously. We developed evolution-inspired multi-objective Bayesian optimization (EvoMOBO), an active-learning framework that integrates path-dependent sequence generation, global candidate competition, and explicit multi-objective optimization, enabling efficient prioritization of high-value variants without exhaustive library enumeration. Compared with state-of-the-art methods on complete steroid receptor DNA-binding domain (DBD) and ParD3 antitoxin landscapes, EvoMOBO achieved greater target-region enrichment while maintaining sequence diversity across two- and three-objective tasks. In the DBD landscape, optimization guided by simulation-derived geometric descriptors enriched variants with satisfactory experimental performance without experimental labels. Building on this validation, we applied EvoMOBO to two enzyme-engineering tasks using mechanistic descriptors, with experiments reserved for final validation. For an old yellow enzyme from Geobacillus kaustophilus, probabilities of substrate binding and reaction preorganization guided optimization of a non-native oxidative dehydrogenation, yielding a variant that increased substrate conversion from 17.5% to 95%. For a formate oxidase from Aspergillus oryzae, stability-related descriptors identified aggregation-resistant variants that nearly doubled diethyl phthalate degradation in a photoenzymatic cascade. Together, these results demonstrate robust multi-objective optimization by EvoMOBO and show that mechanism-derived descriptors can effectively guide protein engineering toward experimentally improved functions.

title: Single-cell and spatial transcriptome analyses unveil that MYH11 links stemness to immunotherapy resistance in non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Xie, Yujie; Xue, Yinyin; Lai, Dongmei; Zhang, Xiang; Li, Guosheng; Zhou, Qinghua
abstract: BACKGROUND: Immunotherapy is an essential treatment strategy for lung cancer, yet resistance to it is often unavoidable, resulting in treatment failure and poor prognosis. The cancer stem cell (CSC) theory offers a valuable perspective for understanding tumor metastasis and resistance to immunotherapy. However, there is a scarcity of multi-omics studies that identify tumor stemness subpopulations and their associated signaling pathways. In this study, we combined single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) with spatial transcriptomics sequencing (ST-seq) to identify a myosin heavy chain 11 (MYH11)-high stemness subpopulation linked to immunotherapy resistance. METHODS: We conducted quality control and removed batch effects from two scRNA-seq datasets, then annotated cell types using established marker genes. Malignant cells were distinguished from epithelial cells with fastCNV. Stemness subpopulations were identified using a machine learning-derived messenger RNA (mRNA) stemness index (mRNAsi) and CytoTRACE analysis. To functionally characterize the stemness subpopulation, we employed Monocle3 pseudotime trajectory analysis, CellChat cell-cell communication analysis, and predicted transcription factors (TFs). We also performed consensus clustering on bulk RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data, followed by immune-related scoring, immune cell deconvolution, and drug sensitivity prediction. Clinical validation was achieved through multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) and immunohistochemistry (IHC). Experimental validation included short hairpin RNA (shRNA)-mediated MYH11 knockdown, real-time quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) and western blot analyses, and tumor sphere formation assays to assess cancer stemness. RESULTS: We identified nine major cell types and found a significant enrichment of epithelial cells in tumors resistant to immunotherapy. Using fastCNV, we identified malignant cells and defined seven malignant cell subtypes based on stemness scoring. Notably, the Stem-subtype was significantly enriched in resistant tumors. Functional analysis showed that the Stem-subtype could differentiate into other malignant cell subtypes, with a strong enrichment in the NOTCH signaling pathway. Analysis of fibroblast subpopulations revealed that MYH11 (+) fibroblasts were closely linked to the Stem-subtype, collectively contributing to immunotherapy resistance. Consensus clustering identified two stemness-related subtypes, with Stemness I associated with poor prognosis. Immune scoring and immune cell analysis further indicated an unfavorable response to immunotherapy in Stemness I. Drug sensitivity prediction identified potential therapeutic agents, and in silico knockout experiments revealed downstream target genes. Validation with clinical samples confirmed that MYH11-high cancer cells were closely correlated with exhausted CD8(+) T cell infiltration and poor immunotherapy outcomes. Experimental validation demonstrated that MYH11 knockdown significantly reduced the expression levels of CXCL12 and TUBA1A, as well as the expression of core NOTCH pathway genes. Furthermore, the tumor sphere-forming capacity was markedly suppressed. CONCLUSIONS: In summary, our multi-omics analysis revealed a MYH11-high malignant cell stemness subpopulation and a MYH11 (+) fibroblast subpopulation, both of which are closely linked to immunotherapy resistance and poor prognosis in lung cancer.

title: Smokeless Tobacco-Associated Nitrosamines Impact on Aryl Hydrocarbon Receptor: In Silico and In Vitro Study.
authors: Sajid, Mohammad; Verma, Ved Vrat; Rawat, Varun; Srivastava, Sonal; Sharma, Pragya; Bharadwaj, Mausumi
journal: Journal of biochemical and molecular toxicology
abstract: Smokeless tobacco (SLT) consumption is a potential health threat around the globe, predominantly in South Asian Countries. SLT products contain several carcinogens, most notably including tobacco-specific nitrosamines (TSNAs). Aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), significantly higher in oral squamous cell carcinoma, is responsible for the recognition of toxic compounds and their elimination by increasing the expression of Cytochrome-P450 enzymes. However, the impact of TSNAs on AhR and AhR-related pathways remains unclear. In this work, we investigate the interaction between AhR and various TSNAs present in SLT products by molecular docking and further validate the effects of aqueous extracts (STEs) of these three SLT products on oral cancer cells (CAL-27) and human embryonic kidney cells (HEK-293). TSNA molecules docked at the classical 2,3,7,8-tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin (TCDD) binding site of AhR. The docking results revealed the comparative binding affinity of all TSNAs molecules against AhR. Accordingly, agonist TCDD and NAT showed the highest and lowest binding affinity against AhR, respectively. Furthermore, STE exposure led to an increase in cell proliferation at low doses, whereas at high doses, inhibition of proliferation was observed against both cell lines. STE treatment showed an increase in ROS production at low doses, indicating cell transformation. AhR and AhR-dependent gene (CYP1A1, CYP1B1, Arnt, and GST) expressions were elevated upon exposure to STE. Therefore, induction of the AhR signalling network by STE exposure may be pathogenetically involved in oral carcinogenesis and future research on designing an appropriate inhibitor against AhR during SLT consumption can assist in the management of oral cancer.

title: Trimetazidine hydrochloride-induced seed germination can effectively alleviate drought stress and salt stress damage in rapeseed seedlings.
authors: Long, Jinjia; Xu, Benbo; Xu, Jinsong; Zhang, Xuekun
abstract: Drought and salt stress are major constraints limiting rapeseed yield and production. Trimetazidine hydrochloride (TMZ) is a metabolic regulator. Previous studies showed that TMZ treatment significantly activated the antioxidant system in rapeseed. In this study, we investigated the effects of different concentrations of TMZ on drought and salt stress tolerance in germinating oilseed rape via phenotypic, physiological and transcriptomic analyses. Results showed that seed priming with TMZ for 7 days significantly inhibited rapeseed growth. Seeds were germinated under TMZ induction for 3 days to cotyledon emergence, followed by drought and salt stress simulation using 20% PEG-6000 and 200 mmol/L NaCl. TMZ priming notably enhanced seedling stress tolerance, with 80 mg/L being the most effective. After seed germination at this concentration under drought stress, the seedling water content increased by 28.49%, while the relative electrical conductivity decreased by 72.83%, compared with seedlings germinated with clean water. Under salt stress, th​e malondialdehyde (MDA) content and relative ​conductivity of seedlings were reduced by 35.64% and 61.34%, respectively, relative to the clear water germination control. TMZ treatment alone also significantly activated the antioxidant system. Time-series transcriptome analysis showed that differentially expressed genes (DEGs) at CK vs. Q12 group were enriched in photosynthesis, energy metabolism, phenylpropanoid biosynthesis, and signal transduction. TMZ repressed auxin (IAA) and gibberellin (GA) signaling but promoted jasmonic acid (JA) pathway. Transcription factor (TF) analysis showed that MYB-related was the largest TF family in both CK vs. Q4 group and CK vs. Q12 group, CCA1 was identified as the core hub gene.

title: Identifying potential targets in endothelial to mesenchymal transition-mediated atherosclerosis using bioinformatics and machine learning.
authors: Hou, Zhengjun; Chen, Sihan; Cui, Yuliang; Ma, Qinfeng; Chen, Jiandong; Shu, Kunxian
abstract: BACKGROUND: Endothelial to mesenchymal transition (EndMT) is a key driver of atherosclerosis (AS). This study integrated multiple RNA transcriptomic and single-cell transcriptomic datasets to identify shared gene expression signatures between EndMT and AS. METHODS: GEO expression profiles were analyzed via differential expression, weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA), and functional enrichment analyses. A Random Forest model evaluated key genes, validating their expression and diagnostic performance. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) further assessed their expression patterns, and a Transcription Factor (TF)-mRNA-miRNA regulatory network. RESULTS: Fifteen overlapping genes were identified, from which six candidates were screened through a Protein-Protein Interaction (PPI) network and validated in vitro. The application of a Random Forest model identified two key hub genes, CCL5 and IL1B, which were significantly upregulated. Their diagnostic Area Under the Curve (AUC) was >0.7 when assessed separately and increased to >0.85 in a combined model. Three shared TFs (NFKBIA, NFKB1, RELA) of the Nuclear Factor-kappa B (NF-kappaB) pathway were identified, highlighting its central role in disease progression. CONCLUSIONS: CCL5 and IL1B are key genes potentially regulating EndMT-mediated AS via inflammatory pathways including Nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain-like (NOD-like) receptor, Tumor Necrosis Factor (TNF), and NF-kappaB signaling, offering promising diagnostic and therapeutic targets for AS.

title: Transcriptomic Identification of Candidate Biomarkers Associated With Vascular Calcification-Related Signaling Pathways in Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy.
authors: Cheng, LiJuan; Xin, ZiJin; Zhao, XinLi; Wang, JingFeng
abstract: BACKGROUND: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) is one of the most prevalent primary glomerular diseases globally. This study is aimed at identifying candidate biomarkers associated with vascular calcification-related signaling pathways in IgAN and at investigating their potential biological associations. METHODS: This was an observational bioinformatics study based on public transcriptomic datasets. Vascular calcification-related genes (VCRGs) were defined based on selected KEGG signaling pathways. Data were obtained from public databases. Candidate biomarkers were identified via differential analysis, machine learning, and cross-compartment external expression assessment. Enrichment analysis, immune infiltration, regulatory networks, computational drug prediction, and computational N6-methyladenosine (m6A) site prediction were used to explore the potential biological context of the candidate biomarkers. RESULTS: Differential analysis identified 348 differentially expressed genes (DEGs). By intersecting these DEGs with VCRGs, 30 candidate genes were obtained. JUN, FOS, and COL1A2 were finally identified as candidate biomarkers, and these genes were mainly associated with the "Nagashima EGF signaling" and "Nagashima NRG1 signaling." Six differential immune cell types (e.g., M2 macrophages) differed significantly between the IgAN and control groups. Spearman analysis showed that COL1A2 was negatively correlated with resting natural killer (NK) cells (cor = -0.57, p < 0.05); and FOS was positively correlated with resting NK cells (cor = 0.72, p < 0.01). BRD4, MAZ, and CTCF were computationally predicted as shared candidate transcription factors (TFs). A regulatory association involving hsa-miR-139-5p and FOS was also predicted. Troglitazone was predicted to target JUN. High-confidence m6A modification sites were computationally predicted in all three candidate biomarkers. These findings were considered exploratory and hypothesis generating. CONCLUSION: JUN, FOS, and COL1A2 were identified as IgAN-associated candidate biomarkers linked to vascular calcification-related signaling pathway genes, providing exploratory biological insights into the potential molecular links between IgAN and calcification-related signaling.

title: Carbonic anhydrase 4 restrains dual TLR4-NF-kappaB/IRF3 innate immune signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition in methotrexate-induced pulmonary fibrosis.
authors: Liu, Ying; Fan, Rui
abstract: BACKGROUND: Methotrexate (MTX)-induced pulmonary fibrosis (MTX-PF) is the most severe and frequently irreversible manifestation of MTX pulmonary toxicity, yet the molecular target and signaling circuitry linking drug exposure to fibrosis remain undefined, hampering diagnosis and targeted intervention. METHODS: We integrated network toxicology, an ensemble of 112 machine-learning classifiers and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) with six GEO cohorts to nominate fibrotic-lung genes, which were intersected with predicted MTX targets to prioritize candidates relevant to MTX-PF. Lead candidates were validated by molecular docking, 100-ns molecular dynamics simulation, MM-PBSA binding free energy calculation and surface plasmon resonance (SPR). In vivo MTX-induced mouse models and in vitro BEAS-2B assays, including the Transwell migration/invasion, EdU proliferation, immunofluorescence, RT-qPCR, Western blotting, CA4 and TLR4 overexpression, and a CA4/TLR4 co-overexpression rescue experiment, were performed to assess the regulatory role of the top-ranked gene. RESULTS: Carbonic anhydrase 4 (CA4) ranked first by SHAP importance (0.120) and diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.879); the Ridge model discriminated training and validation cohorts (AUC = 0.930, 0.897 and 0.864). MTX bound stably to CA4 in silico (Vina -7.078 kcal/mol; MM-PBSA DeltaG(bind) -76.5 kJ/mol), and SPR detected concentration-dependent binding to recombinant CA4 (K(D) = 6.25 muM), identifying CA4 as a candidate direct binding partner. In MTX-treated mice, CA4 was downregulated while TLR4, collagen deposition and serum TNF-alpha, IL-6, IL-1beta, IFN-alpha and IFN-beta were elevated. In BEAS-2B cells, CA4 overexpression suppressed migration, invasion and proliferation, reversed MTX-induced upregulation of TLR4, NF-kappaB, IRF3, VIM, FN1 and COL1A1, and restored E-cadherin. Forced TLR4 overexpression reversed the protective effect of CA4 and re-established the inflammatory and mesenchymal phenotype. CONCLUSION: In MTX-PF, MTX directly binds CA4 in vitro. CA4 loss accompanies coordinate upregulation of the TLR4-NF-kappaB/IRF3 axis and an EMT program coupling epithelial injury to fibrogenesis, and CA4 restoration reverses this program in epithelial cells. Although TLR4 gain-of-function abrogated CA4-mediated suppression, its causal necessity remains untested. Given that TLR4 signaling is context-dependent and can facilitate inflammation resolution in some fibrosis models, therapeutic blockade requires careful attention to cell type and timing. CA4 thus represents a candidate molecular correlate and experimental target, pending clinical and in vivo validation.

title: Integrated pharmacology and validation reveal Formononetin upregulates GSTM2 to modulate prostate cancer immune microenvironment via ROS/STAT3-driven chemokine reprogramming.
authors: Yu, Tianlun; Zhou, Yu; He, Fangkai; Wu, Yufan; Tang, Shiyun; Zhu, Zhouhan; Qian, Wei
abstract: BACKGROUND: Prostate cancer (PCa) is responsible for a substantial proportion of male cancer cases worldwide. Biochemical recurrence (BCR) representing a critical challenge in its disease management. Formononetin, a natural isoflavone derived from traditional Chinese medicine, has demonstrated potential anticancer properties. We sought to determine the translational potential of Formononetin-targeted molecules in PCa. METHODS: A list of putative targets of Formononetin were identified through five public databases. Overlapping candidates underwent further refinement using an ensemble of bioinformatics tools, encompassing differential expression profiling, co-expression network construction, and multiple machine-learning classifiers. Docked complexes and complementary analyses were subjected to evaluate the binding stability. To functionally validate GSTM2, we assessed its functional role on PCa cell growth, motility, and invasiveness in vitro, as well as the expression of CXCL10 and CCL22 chemokines. RESULTS: Integrative analysis identified 413 Formononetin targets, with overlapped 335 PCa-associated genes. Through weighted gene co-expression network analysis and differential expression analysis, 22 candidate genes were identified as Formononetin-related genes in PCa. Machine learning algorithms and survival analysis further suggested GSTM2 as the most important target. GSTM2 was positively correlated with enhanced immune infiltration and sensitivity to Bicalutamide. Single-cell analysis revealed that GSTM2-positive malignant cells exhibited upregulated glutathione metabolism and suppressed respiratory burst pathways. Stable complex formation between Formononetin and GSTM2 was demonstrated by computational docking. Cell-based assays demonstrated that Formononetin upregulated GSTM2 and inhibited PCa malignancy in a GSTM2-required manner. In terms of mechanism, Formononetin attenuated ROS levels and suppressed STAT3 phosphorylation via GSTM2, leading to reprogramming of chemokine expression characterized by upregulated CXCL10 and downregulated CCL22. CONCLUSION: Formononetin reprograms chemokine expression through the GSTM2-ROS-STAT3 axis to regulate the immune microenvironment, suggesting that it might have immune-modulating effects and is worth further in vivo studies.

title: SP1 tethers NR2F2 to drive atrial cardiomyocyte identity.
authors: Gergen, Payton N; Clark, Alexander P; Saucerman, Jeffrey J
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Human heart development is guided by complex gene regulatory networks (GRNs), which are difficult to unravel and differ from that in animal models. In this study, we use a systematic approach to identify gene interactions driving human fetal atrial cardiomyocyte identity. We inferred GRNs for atrial and ventricular cardiomyocytes from human fetal single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq data, predicting transcription factors that differentially regulate atrial vs. ventricular cardiomyocyte identity. Comparison of GRNs constrained by ATAC-seq vs. promoter annotations revealed that during human heart development, the canonical transcription factor for atrial specification, NR2F2, drives atrial genes not directly but by interacting with SP1. The predicted NR2F2-SP1 relationship at atrial gene promoters was supported with AlphaFold predictions of biophysical tethering and comparison with previous ChIP-seq data. These predictions were experimentally validated in human iPSC-derived atrial cardiomyocyte differentiation, which was suppressed by SP1 knockdown. Further, proximity ligation experiments validated the physical interaction of NR2F2 and SP1 in the nucleus, coincident with atrial identity. This study reveals SP1 as a transcription factor necessary for atrial cardiomyocyte identity in human development, helping to coordinate the effects of NR2F2. Furthermore, comparing GRNs based on current and potential epigenetic state offers a novel systematic approach to study interactions between transcription factors, which is key to understanding complex GRNs.

title: Design of synthetic activators for programmable gene expression.
authors: Chen, Wei; Jiao, Ruopu; Coventry, Brian; Qu, Xiangli; Bauer, Magnus; Tran, Long; Tcheau, Tabitha; Wu, Kejia; Song, Zihao; Roullier, Nicole; Li, Xinting; Glasscock, Cameron; Hilton, Isaac B; Baker, David
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Transcription factors control gene expression by recruiting transcriptional coactivators through intrinsically disordered transcriptional activation domains (TADs), whose weak and promiscuous interactions make it difficult to establish quantitative relationships between coactivator recruitment and transcriptional output, and to precisely modulate gene expression. To overcome this limitation, we set out to design coactivator-recruiting proteins using AlphaFold3-predicted TAD-coactivator interactions as a guide. We developed a high-throughput functional screening platform in mammalian cells and identified over 300 well folded nanomolar affinity binders to the transcription coactivators Mediator (multiple subunits), BRD4, NCOA, and p300; targeted interface mutations enabled systematic tuning of their binding affinities. Using a panel of p300 binders spanning nanomolar to micromolar affinities, we found an ultrasensitive relationship between coactivator-binding affinity and transcriptional output, with a sharp transcriptional activation threshold at  approximately 500 nM. Incorporating p300 binder designs into CRISPRa yielded compact synthetic effectors that drove stronger activation than VPR across multiple genomic loci with minimal detectable cytotoxicity. Combining p300- and Mediator-specific binders further enhanced transcription, revealing functional synergy between these coactivators. Together, our work establishes a quantitative framework linking coactivator-binding affinity to transcriptional output and provides compact synthetic effectors for programmable gene activation.

title: Why don't transcription factors exploit inter-nucleotide correlations in binding motifs? Evolution of information encoding strategies on DNA
authors: Emmanuel Mekasha; Elia Mascolo; Ivan Erill
abstract: Transcription factors have been shown to predominantly rely on independent contributions from each position of their target sequence motifs, even though sequence motifs can encode information through correlations among nucleotide positions. As a result, the position-weight matrix, a simple modeling approach that assumes independence among positions, has long since become the dominant model of TF-DNA binding. Why evolution would favor this comparatively simple strategy, known as single locus information (SI), over a correlation-based one remains unaddressed. Here, we use analytical derivations, numerical approaches and evolutionary simulations to show that SI is intrinsically more robust to mutation than correlated (multi-locus) encodings and is therefore indirectly favored under selection for functional transcriptional regulatory networks. At the same time, we show that SI smooths the affinity landscape, ensuring the evolvability of regulatory interactions. We find the same marked bias toward SI in the genetic code, suggesting that the preference for SI is not specific to transcriptional regulation, but may be a general property of biological codes that must reliably store information on DNA in the face of mutational noise.

title: RNA Small-Molecule Binding-Site Prediction by Integrating RNA Language Models and Structural Geometry
authors: Nandita Sharma; Pralay Mitra
abstract: RNAs are emerging as promising therapeutic targets, and small-molecule binding can modulate their structure and function, creating opportunities for therapeutic development. Accurate identification of RNA–small-molecule binding sites is therefore important for understanding RNA–ligand interactions and facilitating RNA-targeted drug discovery. However, the structural complexity of RNA and the limited availability of experimentally characterized RNA–ligand complexes pose challenges for computational binding-site prediction. In this study, we propose RSMBind, a graph attention-based deep learning framework for nucleotide-level prediction of RNA–small-molecule binding sites. The model integrates geometric descriptors of the local three-dimensional environment with pretrained RNA language model embeddings to capture complementary structural and sequence information. We investigate three pretrained RNA language models—RNA-BERT, ERNIE-RNA and RNA-FM—and assess the contributions of sequence representations and geometric features through feature-level ablation experiments. The model is developed using the TR60 and HARIBOSS datasets and evaluated on four independent benchmark datasets: RB9, TE18, TL12 and JL10. RSMBind achieves the highest MCC among the compared methods on three of the four benchmarks, with relative improvements of 17.1% on RB9, 7.2% on TL12 and 16.0% on JL10 over the best previously reported results, while achieving competitive performance on TE18. Furthermore, RSMBind retains predictive capability when using only pretrained RNA language model embeddings, highlighting their potential utility when explicit tertiary structural features are unavailable. Structural analysis indicates differences in prediction performance across RNA structural regions, with loop-associated binding sites generally being captured more effectively than those embedded within stem regions. Additionally, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulations of selected RNA–ligand complexes provide insights into the relationship between predicted binding probabilities and dynamic ligand proximity, further highlighting the role of conformational dynamics in evaluating structure-based predictions. The source code is available at [ https://github.com/sharma-nandita/RSMBind ].

title: ModBERT: a DNA modification and genetic variant-aware DNA large language model
authors: Dante Bolzan; Ramana V Davuluri; Shaun Mahony; FERHAT AY
abstract: The development of foundation models that learn a general grammar of DNA (DNA language models) has accelerated in recent years. The vast majority of DNA large language models (LLMs), such as DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer, are pretrained almost exclusively on reference genomes. They therefore cannot represent the two sources of variation most directly tied to regulatory differences between people: genetic variants and DNA methylation. Long-read sequencing (Nanopore and PacBio) now measures both from the same native DNA molecules, but no model is designed to use this joint readout. With this in mind, we developed ModBERT, a DNA language model built on a five-letter probabilistic genome representation in which each position is a distribution over A, C, G, T, 5mC (represented with M). In pretraining, these distributions encode population allele frequencies and CpG methylation levels from 242 individuals in the 1000 Genomes Long-Read Sequencing Consortium, learned with a soft-target masked language modeling objective. We further propose probabilistic fine-tuning, in which the same representation encodes one individual's genotype and methylation. A fine-tuned model can then make person-specific predictions from a single assay. Under this novel fine-tuning framework, we show that ModBERT effectively utilizes methylation information to classify peaks from functional genomic assays, including histone mark (n=11 different marks) and transcription factor binding (n=69 TFs) ChIP-seq data, outperforming ab initio trained models and ModBERT pretrained on sequences without methylation. In silico methylation perturbations yield TF sensitivities that correlate with independent methylation-aware motif models. Using an evaluation design that separates generalization to new loci from generalization to new individuals, ModBERT predicts chromatin accessibility at held-out loci in held-out individuals (AUROC 0.88). Its predicted variant effects agree with likely causal caQTLs (Spearman correlation = 0.52) but not with variants associated only through linkage, a traditionally challenging task. Overall, ModBERT establishes a framework for personal-genome language modeling, in which a model reads each individual's genetic and epigenetic sequence rather than a shared reference. This enables in silico dissection of variant and methylation effects on gene regulation and principled prioritization of candidates for experimental validation as population-scale long-read cohorts (e.g., 1KGP and Human Pangenome Reference Consortium) grow.

title: CPDD: Adapting an autoregressive DNA language model for bidirectional phage genome modeling
authors: Hao Ding; Nannan Wu; Tianyi Qiu
abstract: Autoregressive DNA language models generate sequences efficiently from left to right, but many genome-analysis and sequence-editing problems are naturally conditioned on both flanks. We introduce CreatiPhage , a 144.5M-parameter autoregressive DNA language model for bacteriophages, and its diffusion extension, CreatiPhage Diffusion DNA-LM (CPDD) . CPDD is a 147.5M-parameter bidirectional discrete diffusion model initialized from the six-epoch CreatiPhage checkpoint. CPDD retains the pretrained Transformer, block attention residuals, and Engram conditional memory, while introducing non-causal attention, a MASK-aware base-5 Engram, centered depthwise convolution, and position-aligned nucleotide readout. Training combines masked and GIDD-style uniformly substituted bases with nucleotide- and amino-acid-level losses over a 10 kb, 32 kb, and whole-source context curriculum. On a screened panel of 522 phage CDSs, CPDD achieves higher random-mask restoration accuracy than a comparable diffusion model and performs well above codon-level references. In a mixed-corruption test, it restores 42.4% of visible incorrect bases. Frozen CPDD representations also support infA fitness prediction and seven-class phage virion protein subtype classification. Controlled evaluations further characterize how restoration depends on visible context and identify opportunities to improve longer-range sequence recovery. Together, these results support scaffold-conditioned sequence modeling as a step towards modular design of phage genomes.

title: Nucleobase-Specific Recognition of DNA by Protamine
authors: Dhiman A; Mudiyanselage HE; Zhou H
abstract: Protamines—arginine (Arg)-rich, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs)—replace histones to compact DNA in the sperm nucleus. While folded domains can bind DNA site-specifically, whether IDPs exhibit DNA-sequence specificity remains open. Here, we used all-atom molecular dynamics simulations to characterize protamine-DNA binding. Eight copies of salmon protamine (33 residues with 21 Arg) rapidly wrap around a 35-bp DNA molecule. In addition to salt bridges with DNA phosphates, Arg hydrogen-bonds with multiple nucleobases on both strands or the same strand. At the major groove, protamine prefers GC over AT by a 2.6-to-1 ratio, with guanine's O6 and N7 atoms as hydrogen-bond acceptors; the preference is especially strong at G-tracts. This selectivity reverses at the minor groove, where AT overtakes GC by a 2.1-to-1 margin. The net effect is a moderate bias for GC over AT in protamine-base interactions. Additional simulations with 20-bp DNA molecules and free-energy calculations reinforce these observations. For experimental validation, we designed DNA sequences with 0–40% GC content. Protamine-DNA mixtures form aggregates, with an increasing propensity at higher GC content and upon shuffling into G-tracts. This work demonstrates that IDPs can bind DNA in a nucleobase-specific manner, with implications for protamine-mediated transcription silencing and remodeling of paternal chromatin.

title: The SOX9 C-terminus encodes a transferable cBAF-recruitment module for enhancer remodeling and cell-state control
authors: Raghawan AK; Li Z; Huang Y; Wang X; Doan P; Gudipudi AC; Conway C; Kositbovornchai S; Hsiang E; Lie PYP; Cleary JM; Sethi NS
abstract: Transcription factors select genomic targets, but how they recruit chromatin remodelers to convert DNA occupancy into cell-state-specific accessibility remains unclear. Here, we identify an intrinsically disordered SOX9 C-terminal module that recruits SMARCB1-containing canonical BAF (cBAF) to stem-like enhancers that open during APC-mutant adenoma formation. Acute, reversible SOX9 degradation displaces cBAF from ~80% of co-bound enhancers, exceeding effects on pBAF and ncBAF, and collapses accessibility and stem-like identity; SOX9 re-expression restores these features. C-terminal truncation preserves DNA binding but disrupts cBAF engagement and chromatin opening. Enforced SMARCB1 docking to truncated SOX9 partially restores cBAF recruitment, accessibility, stem-like transcription, and organoid self-renewal, identifying remodeler recruitment as a limiting effector function. The isolated C-terminus supports higher-order cBAF assembly and, when fused to dCas9 as COMET, redirects endogenous cBAF to targeted loci to open chromatin. Disordered TF regions can therefore encode transferable instructions that deploy specific remodeling complexes to control cell state.

title: Fine-Tuning a Graph-Transformer ADMET Model Improves Half-Life and Plasma Protein Binding Concordance
authors: Basel Mansour; Chetan Anand P; Binil Benny; Sifat Ahmed; Shayoni Dutta; Daniel Kei Takahashi
abstract: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) models are usually judged on predefined benchmark splits. Those splits are useful, but they do not show whether a model reproduces the pharmacokinetic (PK) numbers that are actually reported for individual drugs. Here we compared ADMET-AI with a fine-tuned NV-KERMT-70M-v2 model (“KERMT”) on the same Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC)-aligned endpoint definitions. KERMT was fine-tuned in two stages: a protocol check on the ChEMBL multitask (ChEMBL-MT) data set, then TDC-aligned regression and classification fine-tuning on merged ChEMBL, Biogen, ExpansionRx/OpenADMET and TDC data. Two retrospective literature comparisons were run. The first used a curated 25-drug oncology panel: for half-life (n = 17) KERMT cut mean absolute error (MAE) from 46.81 to 16.83 h (paired Wilcoxon p = 0.0046, Holm-adjusted p = 0.0139, closer for 13 of 17 drugs); volume of distribution at steady state (VDss, n = 12) and hepatocyte clearance (n = 17) showed no statistically supported difference. The second, reported here for the first time, is an expanded three-way comparison of 53 oncology drugs × 3 endpoints (159 drug-endpoint rows) against curated literature and label values. On the 48 drugs with a usable half-life reference, KERMT more than halved the error (MAE 19.43 vs 43.38 h; median absolute error 12.01 vs 35.30 h; geometric mean fold error, GMFE, 2.72 vs 3.69; within 2-fold 41.0% vs 25.0%), was closer for 34 of 48 drugs (70.8%; 95% confidence interval, CI, 55.9-83.0%), and the paired Wilcoxon test was significant (p = 0.0002; Holm-adjusted p = 0.0004). The advantage persisted after each model's systematic bias was removed (p = 0.0004), so it is not a simple scale offset: ADMET-AI over-predicted half-life for 35 of 48 drugs (mean bias +29.20 h) whereas KERMT was mildly conservative (-13.79 h). For plasma protein binding ratio (PPBR, n = 21) KERMT had lower MAE (7.05 vs 9.44 percentage points) and the only statistically significant rank agreement with literature seen anywhere in this study (Spearman ρ = 0.540, p = 0.012, vs 0.400, p = 0.073), but the paired error difference was not significant (p = 0.157). One endpoint failed outright and we state it plainly: KERMT VDss predictions collapsed to near-baseline behaviour. They occupied a narrow band (46 of 53 drugs between 0 and 10 L/kg; standard deviation 3.64 vs 6.71 L/kg for ADMET-AI), no drug in the panel had an assay-matched VDss reference, and on the six drugs with an approximate reference the per-drug KERMT predictions (MAE 2.18 L/kg) were no better than replacing the entire model with one constant (MAE 2.14 L/kg) and worse than a no-information baseline (1.71 L/kg). KERMT VDss output should therefore not be used. A deliberately strict control bounds the positive findings as well: against a structure-blind constant predictor built by leave-one-out from the reference values, KERMT was statistically indistinguishable on both endpoints (half-life MAE 19.43 vs 16.07 h, p = 0.051; PPBR 7.05 vs 7.24 percentage points, p = 0.812), while ADMET-AI was significantly worse than that constant for half-life (p < 0.0001). We therefore make no claim of accurate numerical point prediction; the supported claims are that fine-tuning removes ADMET-AI's large systematic half-life error and that the PPBR rank correlation is compound-specific signal a constant cannot possess. Physically impossible values occurred in 16 of 159 KERMT rows and 21 of 159 ADMET-AI rows. Across 30 classification endpoints, mean inter-model Pearson correlation was 0.711 and mean binary agreement at 0.5 was 89%, which measures similarity, not accuracy. This version does not yet include official Therapeutics Data Commons benchmark-group evaluation of the fine-tuned models, replicate training seeds, or a training-set overlap audit; those gaps are declared explicitly rather than left implicit. The overall conclusion is endpoint-specific: fine-tuned KERMT is a materially better-calibrated half-life and plasma-protein-binding predictor than ADMET-AI on this panel, it is not yet a demonstrated ranking model for half-life, and its VDss head is unusable.
